      # SessionStart command uses an absolute ~/.claude path so the hook fires
      # regardless, but `herdr integration status` probes CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR
      # (a profile dir under claude-prof) for <dir>/hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh
      # — symlink it in so status reads "current" per profile too.
      [ -d "$HOME/.claude/hooks" ] && [ ! -e "$dir/hooks" ] && ln -sf "$HOME/.claude/hooks" "$dir/hooks"
      # skills/ holds the personal (non-plugin) skills rendered by home.file
      # above. Claude resolves user skills only under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, so
      # without this link every profile sees an empty skill set and ~/.claude
      # is the sole profile that can run them.
      [ -d "$HOME/.claude/skills" ] && [ ! -e "$dir/skills" ] && ln -sf "$HOME/.claude/skills" "$dir/skills"
    done
  '';

  # Firefox 67+ keys profile-per-install via [Install<HASH>] sections in
  # profiles.ini (gated by `Version=2`), overriding `Default=1`. Every nix
  # firefox bump makes a new install hash, so Firefox creates a fresh
  # *.default-release profile and pins it, ignoring the home-manager one.
  # Dropping Version= makes Firefox honor Default=1 (like Darwin); rm the legacy
  # installs.ini backup so it can't re-seed the Install section on next launch.
  home.activation.firefoxInstallsIni = lib.hm.dag.entryAfter [ "writeBoundary" ] ''
    $DRY_RUN_CMD rm -f "$HOME/${config.programs.firefox.configPath}/installs.ini"

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

browser: install zen in place of firefox

Zen is not in nixpkgs, so it comes from the community flake
(0xc000022070/zen-browser-flake), whose home-manager module is generated by
home-manager's own mkFirefoxModule -- the same generator behind
programs.firefox. That is what makes this a move rather than a rewrite:
policies, profileVersion, nativeMessagingHosts and profiles.<n>.settings all
mean what they meant, so the block below is the firefox block with two
deletions.

Dropped along the way:

- configPath. The firefox block pinned .mozilla/firefox because env.nix sets
  MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES=1. Zen does not need the override: its application.ini
  carries `Profile=zen` and the wrapped binary lands on ~/.config/zen, the
  module default, even with the var set. Checked by running zen-beta 1.22.3b
  (gecko 156) under a throwaway $HOME with MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES=1 -- it created
  ~/.config/zen, not ~/.zen. The var stays for thunderbird, which does read the
  legacy layout.
- sidebar.verticalTabs. That pref drives Firefox's vertical tab strip, which
  Zen replaces outright with its sidebar; Zen's equivalents are zen.* prefs.

Kept: the Homepage policy, tridactyl-native as a native messaging host, the
bitwarden + tridactyl addons from rycee's NUR set (same extension IDs, same
gecko), and every other pref including the http3 third-party-roots workaround.
profileVersion = null and the installs.ini activation carry over for the same
reason they existed -- gecko 67+ pins profile-per-install via [Install<HASH>]
and every nix bump mints a new hash -- with the activation's path no longer
$HOME-prefixed, because zen-browser's configPath is absolute.

BROWSER and the http/https/text-html mime defaults now name zen-beta /
zen-beta.desktop: upstream calls its stable channel "beta" and the flake names
the wrapper and desktop entry after the channel. BROWSER is set in env.nix
rather than through the module's setAsDefaultBrowser, which would collide on
that same option.

mari moves too, on the module's default darwin.packageMode = "signed" (upstream
.app untouched, so its Team ID integrations keep working). All six host configs
evaluate; extensions stay Linux-only, as under firefox.

Known gap: bitwarden-desktop writes its native messaging manifest to
~/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts, which Zen does not read, so biometric unlock
will want that manifest linked into ~/.config/zen/native-messaging-hosts.
Noted at the bitwarden-desktop package, not fixed here.

Correcting it:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import io
p='home.nix'; s=io.open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
old='''    # Desktop app is the biometric backend the browser extension talks to over
    # native messaging (the extension can't unlock with biometrics on its own).
    # NOTE: it writes its own manifest to ~/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts, a
    # path Zen does not read (~/.config/zen/native-messaging-hosts) - expect
    # biometric unlock to need that manifest linked across.
    # Pairs with the polkit action + pam_fprintd wiring in system/.'''
new='''    # Desktop app is the biometric backend the browser extension talks to over
    # native messaging (the extension can't unlock with biometrics on its own).
    # Survived the move off firefox: gecko reads native manifests from
    # XREUserNativeManifests + /native-messaging-hosts, and that base is a
    # hardcoded ~/.mozilla on Linux for every gecko app -- so the manifest
    # bitwarden-desktop writes there is the one Zen loads, and the zen wrapper
    # symlinks tridactyl's beside it at launch.
    # Pairs with the polkit action + pam_fprintd wiring in system/.'''
assert s.count(old)==1, s.count(old)
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s.replace(old,new))
print('ok')
PY

result.output:
Spawn one review panel for `task`, wait, merge, exit 0/3/2/1.

Two forms:

```text drovr code-review run <RUN> <TASK>                    # inside a pipeline run drovr code-review run --base <rev> [--dir <repo>] <TASK>   # anywhere else ```

The second exists because `drovr:code-review` is unconditional while `drovr:using-drovr`'s escalation contract says to work INLINE until the work outgrows one context — so the agent that followed the contract correctly was the one with no run, and no way to review its change (forge#108). `--base` supplies what `<TASK>-base.sha` supplies in a run, so nothing has to have been recorded before the first edit: after the fact you know your own branch point, `git merge-base HEAD main`. `--dir` defaults to the current directory.

The panel, the brief, the resume and the merged findings are identical between the two; only the ADDRESSING changes. The runless form keeps its artifacts in a run dir derived from the repo path and the task, which is what lets a resume find them — see `code_review::ephemeral_review_run`. It appears in `drovr list` as `cr-<task>-<hash>` and is torn down with `drovr cleanup`.

Re-running after a timeout (exit 2) RESUMES: it re-attaches to the panel still in flight, banks the angles that finished, and keeps waiting on the stragglers. Pass `--fresh` to abandon them and open a new panel instead.

Usage: drovr code-review run [OPTIONS] <FIRST> [SECOND]

Arguments:
  <FIRST>
          `<RUN>` in the run-scoped form; `<TASK>` when `--base` is given.
          
          One positional carrying two meanings, rather than making `<RUN>` optional: with two optional positionals `run <TASK>` and `run <RUN>` are the same parse, and clap would have to guess which the caller meant. `--base` is the discriminator, and [`Self::review_target`] is the one place that reads it.

  [SECOND]
          `<TASK>` in the run-scoped form. Must be absent with `--base`

Options:
      --base <BASE>
          Review `<base>..HEAD` with no run — the runless form. Anything git resolves: a sha, `main`, `HEAD~3`, or `$(git merge-base HEAD main)`

      --dir <DIR>
          The repository to review, for the runless form. Defaults to the current directory

      --timeout-ms <TIMEOUT_MS>
          How long to wait for the panel, in milliseconds.
          
          Nine minutes, and deliberately NOT `review wait`'s thirty: this command is read in the foreground, and an agent harness kills a foreground shell call at 600 000 ms. The two failures either side of that ceiling are not symmetric, which is why the default sits under it with margin rather than over it. Above the ceiling the reader is killed with 137/143 — a status that is not one of drovr's exit codes, so there is no verdict to read and nothing says whether the panel found anything; forge#93 measured 7 of 23 iterations left unclassifiable that way. Below it the caller gets exit 2 and re-runs, which resumes the same iteration and waits only on the angles still outstanding, so the findings already in are banked rather than re-solicited. A caller that backgrounds the panel is under no such ceiling and passes a longer value explicitly.
          
          [default: 540000]

      --fresh
          Always start a new review iteration, even if a previous one is still in flight. Use when the pending reviewers are wedged or reviewing a diff you no longer care about

Every shell start printed a literal `}}` just before the prompt char.

Ghostty's zsh integration marks multiline prompts by rewriting PS1 as text:
`PS1=${PS1//$'\n'/$'\n'${mark2}}`, where mark2 is `%{\e]133;A;k=s\a%}`. Under

parameter expansion that holds newlines as data inside `${...}` -- so the `}`
inside the spliced mark closes an expansion a level early and the braces after
it fall out as literal text.

Bisecting the generated .zshrc put it on the ghostty source block; p10k alone
is clean, p10k + ghostty-integration is not, and stubbing out only that
newline pass in a copy of the script makes it clean again with the other marks
intact. The insertions land at offsets 6993 and 7206 of p10k's PROMPT.

exactly the one render it breaks. Upstream has the same root cause filed for
the Pure and jreese themes (ghostty-org/ghostty#11407, #11712), both open.

Zen is on all five GUI hosts including mari and off on the two headless ones — `nix eval` confirms: utsuho=on, setsuna=on, shiori=on, mari=on, kyuusaku=off, fujiwara=off. `xdg.mimeApps` touched only the three browser MIME entries; `mailto`/`rfc822` still thunderbird.

      $ cat …-zen-beta-1.22.3b/lib/zen-bin-1.22.3b/distribution/policies.json
      {"policies":{"DisableAppUpdate":true,"DisableTelemetry":true,"Homepage":{…}}}
  
  The nixpkgs firefox wrapper adds no such defaults (wrapper.nix:195-204 adds only `Extensions`/`SecurityDevices`), so under `programs.firefox` `policies.json` carried Homepage only. `DisableTelemetry` flips datareporting prefs. Both are probably wanted, but the commit says "Kept: the Homepage policy … and every other pref" and nothing about the two that appeared — in this repo that is exactly the kind of thing a comment is for.
  
  **Finding 2 — nit (dropped, not carried over).** Under `programs.firefox` the tridactyl manifest was *declarative*: generation 4's home-files contains `.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts/{.keep,tridactyl.json}`, and `~/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts/tridactyl.json` on disk is a store symlink. Under zen, `nix eval` of `config.home.file` shows only `.config/zen/{profiles.ini,default/…}` — no `.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts` at all. Tridactyl native messaging now depends entirely on the wrapper's launch-time `ln -sfLt ~/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts …` (verified in `bin/zen-beta`). The comment does mention the wrapper, so the mechanism is documented, but declarative → launch-time is a semantic downgrade (nothing works until Zen has been launched once) that no comment names.

With firefox dropped outright and no fallback, one sentence saying "profile data is not migrated; `~/.mozilla/firefox` is left behind unmanaged" is the warning this repo's style would carry.

This also means `hms` cannot have run (it refuses a checkout ahead of origin), so nothing in this change has been applied on any host: the commit's claims are eval/build claims only ("All six host configs evaluate and shiori's generation builds"), which is honest, but the runtime claim in Finding 5 below is still untested where it matters. Tree is clean otherwise.

  ### 3. Comment accuracy — one wrong mechanism repeated in two places, one claim fully verified
  
  **Finding 5 — Critical. `home.nix:2909-2914` — the stated mechanism is wrong, and the test cannot support the conclusion.**
  
  Comment: "Zen's application.ini carries `Profile=zen`, and the wrapped binary lands on ~/.config/zen — the module default — even with env.nix's MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES=1 in scope. Checked 2026-09-26 by running zen-beta 1.22.3b under a throwaway $HOME with the var set: it created ~/.config/zen, not ~/.zen."
  
  Three separate problems:
  
  (a) **`MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES` has nothing to do with the profile directory.** `toolkit/profile/nsToolkitProfileService.cpp`:
  
      bool nsToolkitProfileService::UseLegacyProfiles() {
        bool legacyProfiles = !!PR_GetEnv("MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES");
  
  with the comment "This environment variable provides a way to opt out of dedicated profiles". It disables profile-per-install (`[InstallHASH]`), i.e. it does the *same job* as the `profileVersion = null` two lines below. It never selected `~/.mozilla` vs `~/.config`. So the comment rules out a risk that never existed — and, note, the old firefox comment it replaces made the same conflation, so the error was inherited and re-asserted rather than caught.
  
  (b) **`Profile=zen` is the reason it would be `~/.zen`, not the reason it is `~/.config/zen`.** `toolkit/xre/nsXREDirProvider.cpp` `AppendProfilePath`: `if (!aLocal && (IsForceLegacyHome() || LegacyHomeExists(nullptr))) folder.Assign('.');` then appends the application.ini `Profile=` value lowercased. Legacy → `~/.zen`; XDG → `~/.config/zen`. The dot comes from the *mode*, not from `Profile=`. Separately, the file cited says on its own first line: "This file is not used. If you modify it … move it under the browser/ subdirectory" (there is no `browser/application.ini` in this build), so it is weak evidence even for what it does say.
  
  (c) **The real switch is `MOZ_LEGACY_HOME` *or an already-existing legacy dir*, which a throwaway `$HOME` cannot have.** `GetLegacyOrXDGHomePath` takes the legacy branch when `exists || IsForceLegacyHome() || aForceLegacy`, and `LegacyHomeExists` tests the per-app dotted dir *and* falls back to `$HOME/MOZ_USER_DIR`. `MOZ_USER_DIR` is `.mozilla` in a gecko build (libxul here contains exactly one standalone `.mozilla` literal and no `.zen` literal — the `.zen` name is built at runtime), and **this host has `~/.mozilla` (with `~/.mozilla/firefox` in it, and it is not removed by this change)**. A throwaway `$HOME` is precisely the one environment where that branch cannot fire, so the experiment quoted as the evidence is the experiment that cannot detect the failure mode. If the legacy branch does fire on the real host, Zen reads `~/.zen`, and every pref/policy/extension/profiles.ini this block writes to `~/.config/zen` is silently ignored — plus `zenInstallsIni` would `rm` the wrong `installs.ini`. Settle it before/at the switch: launch zen-beta with the real `$HOME` and read **about:support → Profile Directory** (or `about:profiles`); if it shows `~/.zen`, this block needs `configPath` back (or `MOZ_LEGACY_HOME` handling), not a comment fix.

  - "the legacy layout this selects" — same error as Finding 5(a): `MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES` selects non-dedicated profiles, not a directory layout. `~/.thunderbird` comes from thunderbird's own legacy-home/`Profile=` handling, not from this var.
  - "home-manager's thunderbird profile lives in ~/.thunderbird" — true as stated (`modules/programs/thunderbird.nix:55`: `thunderbirdConfigPath = if isDarwin then "Library/Thunderbird" else ".thunderbird"`) and `programs.thunderbird` is indeed enabled here (`home.nix:2835`), so the *existence* half checks out.
  - But the var is redundant for that consumer anyway: nixpkgs' thunderbird is `wrapThunderbird = wrapFirefox` (mailreaders/thunderbird/wrapper.nix), and wrapper.nix:327-333 does `--set MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES 1` **unconditionally** — the same `--set` that is visible in `bin/zen-beta` as `export MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES='1'`. Every nixpkgs-wrapped gecko app gets it regardless of env.nix.
  - And the fallback justification "so does any Arch-packaged gecko app" is moot on this host: `pacman -Q firefox thunderbird` → "not found", `/usr/bin/firefox` and `/usr/bin/thunderbird` do not exist. After dropping firefox there is no known consumer of this variable left.
  
  So the honest note is either "kept defensively; no current consumer — every nixpkgs gecko wrapper sets it itself" or delete the var. As written, the comment asserts a mechanism and a beneficiary that the store contradicts. It also makes Finding 5's framing worse: because the wrapper forces the var, the experiment "with the var set" could not have had any other outcome.
  
  **Finding 7 — verified correct (no action). `home.nix:2103-2107` bitwarden/native-messaging.** This one holds up under checking. `nsXREDirProvider.cpp` resolves `XREUserNativeManifests` via `GetUserDataDirectoryHome(…, /* aLocal */ false, /* aForceLegacy */ true)` and then `file->AppendNative(".mozilla"_ns)` on non-macOS — i.e. the base really is forced-legacy `$HOME/.mozilla` for every gecko app, independent of whether the *profile* is XDG or legacy (nice non-obvious detail to have captured). The wrapper half is verbatim true: `bin/zen-beta` runs `mkdir -p ${MOZ_HOME:-~/.mozilla}/native-messaging-hosts` and `ln -sfLt … tridactyl-native-0.4.1/lib/mozilla/native-messaging-hosts/*`. Two nits: "the manifest bitwarden-desktop writes there" is asserted, not observed — `~/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts/` today holds only HM's `.keep` and `tridactyl.json`, no bitwarden manifest; and see Finding 2 about the declarative→launch-time shift.
  
  **Finding 8 — verified correct. `flake.nix:36` "Not in nixpkgs (checked against this lock)".** `nix eval` against the locked nixpkgs: `has_zen = false; has_zen_beta = false; has_zen_browser = false; has_zenbrowser = false`; no `pkgs/by-name/ze/zen-browser*`, no `zen-browser` in all-packages.nix.   **Finding 9 — nit. `env.nix:84` / `home.nix:3365` "upstream calls the stable channel beta".** Mis-attributed. What is verifiable: the *flake* names the variant `beta` (`flake.nix: homeModules.beta`, `binaryName = "zen-${name}"`, `applicationName … if name == "beta" then " (Beta)"`), and it fetches upstream release tag `1.22.3b` of `zen-browser/desktop` — upstream's own channel names in sources.json are the release tag vs `twilight`. So "the flake names the wrapper and desktop entry after its variant, which tracks upstream's `…b` stable tags" is the defensible wording. The dependent facts are all correct: the package really ships `bin/zen-beta` and `share/applications/zen-beta.desktop` (`Exec=zen-beta --name zen-beta %U`), so the mimeApps values and `BROWSER` resolve.
  
  **Also verified correct (spot-checks worth recording):**
  - `setAsDefaultBrowser` really would collide: `hm-module/default-browser.nix` sets `home.sessionVariables.BROWSER = "zen-beta"` with no `mkDefault`, against env.nix's own `BROWSER` — a genuine conflict. (It would also claim `x-scheme-handler/mailto`, though with `mkDefault`.)
  - `darwin.packageMode` default is `"signed"` (`hm-module/package.nix:99-103`), and upstream's own header names "1Password, iCloud Passwords, Touch ID and Gatekeeper" — so `home.nix:2934-2935`'s "1Password, Touch ID" is a faithful subset, and policies still land on darwin via `defaultsId = "app.zen-browser.zen"` (an `app.zen-browser.zen.plist.drv` exists in the store).
  - "1.22.3b is gecko 156": application.ini `[Gecko] MinVersion=156.0.1`, sources.json `firefoxVersion: "156.0.1"`. ✓
  - The activation is correct and the "absolute configPath" note is right: `configPath` evaluates to `/home/sauyon/.config/zen` (linux) and `…/Library/Application Support/Zen` (darwin), and the built activation is `rm -f "/home/sauyon/.config/zen/installs.ini"`. `home.file` targets are correctly home-relative (HM strips the prefix), and the generated profiles.ini is exactly `[Profile0] Default=1 / IsRelative=1 / Name=default / Path=default` with no `Version=` — the commit's "Default=1 and no Version=" and "policies.json carries the Homepage" both check out.
  - `config.warnings` is empty for shiori (the flake passes `platforms.linux.vendorPath`, but `mkFirefoxModule`'s `vendorPath` option still defaults to null, so the deprecation warning does not fire). No new eval warnings.
  
  ---
  
  ### 4. Style fit + commit message
  
  Style is a good match: em dashes inside `.nix` comments and `--` in the commit body, matching the file; comment width, placement above the option, and option order all preserved; explaining an *absent* option (`configPath`) and an *absent* pref (`sidebar.verticalTabs`) in prose is consistent with how this repo documents removals elsewhere. Subject line is accurate and the body's structure (what moved / what dropped / what was kept / how verified) is the house style.
  
  Commit-message-vs-diff consistency: accurate except where it repeats the comment errors. Specifically: "its application.ini carries `Profile=zen` and the wrapped binary lands on ~/.config/zen … even with the var set" (Findings 5a–5c); "The var stays for thunderbird, which does read the legacy layout" (Finding 6); and "Kept: … and every other pref" omits the two policies the module injects (Finding 1). "the block below is the firefox block with two deletions" is a fair description of the diff. **nit:** the body says "Checked by running zen-beta … under a throwaway $HOME" without flagging that a throwaway `$HOME` is the one place the existing-legacy-home branch can't fire — the repo's own convention is to state what a test could *not* have caught (the ghostty block right below does exactly that, at length).
  
  ---
  
  ### Ratings summary
  
  | # | Rating | Where |
  |---|---|---|
  | 5 | **Critical** | `home.nix:2909-2914` — wrong mechanism (`MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES` = dedicated profiles, not paths; `Profile=zen` implies `~/.zen` under legacy), and the throwaway-`$HOME` test cannot see the `LegacyHomeExists` branch that this host's existing `~/.mozilla` may trigger. Confirm via about:support Profile Directory before trusting `~/.config/zen`. |
  | 6 | Important | `env.nix:43-46` — "the legacy layout this selects" false; the var is forced by every `wrapFirefox` wrapper anyway (wrapper.nix:327-333) and no Arch gecko app exists on this host, so the stated reason to keep it does not hold. |
  | 1 | Important | `home.nix:2921-2926` / commit body — `DisableAppUpdate` + `DisableTelemetry` arrive undeclared from `hm-module/package.nix:215-216`; policy set silently widened vs the firefox block. |
  | 4 | Important | repo rules — `master` is ahead 1; AGENTS.md says always push, CLAUDE.md says commit *and* push. Nothing switched, so Finding 5 is untested on a real host. |
  | 2 | nit | `home.nix:2103-2107` — tridactyl's manifest went from declarative to launch-time-only; no bitwarden manifest exists on disk today, so "keeps working" is asserted. |
  | 3 | nit | no note that the firefox profile is not migrated and `~/.mozilla/firefox` is left behind unmanaged. |
  | 9 | nit | `env.nix:84`, `home.nix:3365` — "upstream calls the stable channel beta" is the flake's naming, not upstream's. |
  | — | nit | commit body omits the limitation of the throwaway-`$HOME` test. |
  
  **Clean categories:** the no-emails rule (nothing but the permitted git identity and the required trailer); scope discipline on the nix options themselves (no gold-plating, exactly the two documented deletions, gating and all six host evals correct); style fit; and the two factual claims in Findings 7 and 8, which I confirmed against gecko source and the locked nixpkgs respectively.

Verified two more: `~/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts/` today holds only HM's `.keep` and `tridactyl.json` (so under firefox tridactyl's manifest was *declarative*; under zen it's the wrapper's launch-time symlink — a real downgrade my comment didn't name, and no bitwarden manifest exists there at all), and there is no Arch-packaged firefox/thunderbird/zen on this host, so env.nix's "any Arch-packaged gecko app" has no current beneficiary.

Confirmed-real findings queued for fixing, all in comments/commit prose rather than nix semantics:

Review of b9eb943 raised, as Critical from two independent reviewers, that Zen
would read ~/.zen rather than ~/.config/zen: gecko 156's LegacyHomeExists()
takes the legacy branch when $HOME/MOZ_USER_DIR exists, MOZ_USER_DIR is
.mozilla, and every host here has ~/.mozilla -- thunderbird's
native-messaging dir alone guarantees it, and zen's own wrapper mkdir's it at
launch. If true, every file the block writes would be unread: prefs,
extensions, profiles.ini, and zenInstallsIni would rm the wrong installs.ini.

It is not true for Zen. Measured against zen-beta 1.22.3b, throwaway $HOME
each time, MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES=1 in scope throughout (the wrapper sets it, so
it cannot be removed from the experiment):

  bare $HOME                      -> ~/.config/zen
  $HOME/.mozilla/firefox present  -> ~/.config/zen   (full launch, not just
                                     -CreateProfile)
  $HOME/.zen present              -> ~/.zen
  MOZ_LEGACY_HOME=1               -> ~/.zen

So the config stays as it is and no configPath comes back. What the reviewers
were right about is the mechanism I had written down: MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES opts
gecko out of dedicated (profile-per-install) mode and has nothing to do with
the directory, and `Profile=zen` is what makes the legacy path ~/.zen rather
than what makes the XDG path ~/.config/zen. The comment now states the switch
(MOZ_LEGACY_HOME, or an existing ~/.zen), carries the table, and says what the
experiment cannot catch -- a distro-packaged Zen or a stray MOZ_LEGACY_HOME
moves the profile silently, symptom is a virgin profile, check about:profiles.

what it actually does and for its one remaining consumer: thunderbird, whose
nixpkgs wrapper is the only gecko wrapper here that does not set the var
itself (0 hits in its launcher, against 1 in zen's). The old note claimed a
layout the var does not select and an Arch-packaged gecko app that is not
installed on these hosts.

commit only documents:

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/systematic-debugging

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**A fix you cannot explain is a guess wearing a diff.** Until the failure
happens on demand and you can say *mechanistically* why, any change you make is
as likely to hide the bug as to remove it. Follow the spirit, not the letter:
running the reproduction once, seeing red, and then fixing what you *assumed*
was wrong satisfies the ordering and proves nothing. The rule is that the cause
you fix is the cause you demonstrated.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** They will not have your hunch, your scrollback, or the shape you
recognized. They get the reproduction command, the cause you wrote down, and the
test you added — anything you only knew is lost at the phase boundary.

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIX BEFORE A REPRODUCTION AND A MECHANISTIC CAUSE.
```

No exceptions:

- **Do not act on a shape you recognize.** A failure matching one you have seen
  before is a reason to *suspect* a cause, not a reason to skip confirming it.
  Go read this instance's fixture, input, or state and confirm it is that bug.
  Recognition works on the assertion output; the bug lives somewhere you have
  not looked yet.
- **Do not read a conditional instruction as permission to skip its condition.**
  *"If it's the off-by-one, just fix it"* waives re-litigating the fix once the
  cause is confirmed — it never waives confirming it. Establish the antecedent
  yourself, then take the permission it grants.
- **Do not let a deadline shorten the verification.** After the fix, re-run the
  original trigger **and** the full suite — the scope
  `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick under time
  pressure. The clock does not change which tests can catch what this fix
  disturbed. If the full suite genuinely cannot be run here, name the exact
  command you did not run and do not report the bug as fixed.
- **Do not start fix #4.** Three *failed fixes* — the unit is defined in step 6 —
  means your model of the system is wrong, not that the fourth guess is due.
  Stop, say so, and question the design with whoever owns it before changing
  another line.
- **Do not substitute reasoning for a reproduction.** If you cannot trigger the
  failure on demand, that is the finding to report. Keep narrowing — smaller
  input, more logging, a read-only explorer — and stop before shipping a fix
  you cannot verify.

## Announce

Say this out loud when you start, before the first edit:

```
Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each bug you work, not once for the session. If you
fall back to `CHECKLIST.md` at a repo root, do not commit it.

1. **Reproduce.** Get a reliable, minimal trigger and record the exact command
   and its output. A bug you cannot reproduce on demand is a bug you cannot
   prove you fixed.
2. **Isolate.** Narrow to the smallest input, file, or code path that still
   shows it. Bisect, add logging, or dispatch a **read-only explorer** to map
   the suspect area. Fan-out investigation belongs to read-only explorers (e.g.
   `explore-mcp`), never to parallel writers — you keep the editing, which is
   what keeps drovr's single-writer rule intact.
3. **Root-cause.** Explain *why* it happens, mechanistically. "Adding this line
   makes it go away" is not a cause. Keep going until the explanation predicts
   the observed behavior exactly — including the parts you were not chasing.
4. **Fix.** Make the minimal change that addresses the cause, not the symptom.
5. **Verify.** Re-run your original trigger and confirm it is gone, then run the
   **full suite** — unconditionally, whatever the clock says.
   `drovr:verification-before-completion` owns what "full" means here and what
   evidence it takes; do not substitute a narrower scope you picked yourself.
   Add or fix a test that would have caught it.
6. **Escalate at three failed fixes.** A **failed fix** is one change you made,
   ran, and watched leave the failure in place. That is the unit — not edits, not
   builds, not ideas you considered and dropped. Count them for this one failure.
   At three, stop and question the design with whoever owns it; do not start fix
   #4 without that conversation. A run of wrong fixes is evidence about your
   model of the system, not about the next fix.

### The cycle

```dot
digraph debugging_loop {
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  repro  [label="reproduce it\non demand", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  story  [label="no trigger —\nyou have a story,\nnot a bug"];
  cause  [label="mechanistic cause", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  fix    [label="minimal fix,\nat the cause", fillcolor=palegreen];
  verify [label="trigger +\nthe full suite", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  stop   [label="three failed fixes —\nquestion the design", fillcolor=lightpink];
  // "failed fix" is procedure step 6's unit: a change made, run, and seen to
  // leave the failure in place.
  done   [label="fixed, with a test\nthat would have caught it"];

  repro  -> story  [label="cannot"];
  story  -> repro  [label="narrow: smaller input,\nlogging, read-only explorer"];
  repro  -> cause  [label="on demand"];
  cause  -> cause  [label="'it goes away' is\nnot a cause"];
  cause  -> fix    [label="predicts the\nobserved behavior"];
  fix    -> verify;
  verify -> done   [label="gone, suite green"];
  verify -> cause  [label="still failing —\ncount one failed fix"];
  verify -> stop   [label="that was the\nthird failed fix"];
}
```

## Red flags — STOP

Some of these are thoughts and some are things you have just observed. Either
way you are at the line, not past it — stop here and the loop is still intact.

- *"We've seen this exact failure before."* · *"They said if it's the off-by-one,
  just fix it."* · *"I'll run the broader suite if time allows."* — each of these
  opens a row in *Rationalizations* below. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are editing code and have not yet run the failing command yourself.* →
  Run it first. What you are fixing is a description of the bug, not the bug.
- *The failure went away and you cannot say why.* → Put the change back and
  confirm it returns. A fix whose mechanism you cannot state may be moving the
  bug rather than removing it.
- *The failure is intermittent, so you will "fix it and watch".* → You have no
  trigger, so you will have no proof. Narrow until it is on demand, or report
  that you could not.
- *You are about to start a fourth fix for the same failure.* → Stop. Three
  failed fixes is the escalation trigger, not a streak to break.
- **Any thought that ends with an edit landing before you can state the cause in
  one sentence.** The reason does not matter and the quality of the reasoning
  does not matter — if you are explaining why the cause can wait, that is the
  red flag.

## Rationalizations

The right-hand column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"We've seen this exact failure before — it's the day-boundary off-by-one."* | Read this instance before you touch it. A prior bug of the same shape is a hypothesis to check, and checking it costs a few minutes, not the afternoon you are protecting. |
| *"They said if it's the off-by-one, just fix it."* | Confirm the antecedent, then take the permission. The conditional waives re-litigating the fix once you have the cause; it does not waive getting the cause. |
| *"The fix works — I don't need to explain why the bug happened."* | State the mechanism now, in one sentence, before you move on. If you cannot, you have a change that correlates with green, and the next agent inherits nothing they can reason from. |
| *"I can't reproduce it, so I'll fix it and see."* | Report that you cannot reproduce it and keep narrowing. Shipping a fix for a failure you never triggered spends someone else's next debugging session on your guess. |
| *"I'll run the broader suite if time allows."* | Run the full suite before you report — the scope `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick now. The deadline changes what you can finish; it does not change which tests can catch what this fix disturbed. Cut scope somewhere it is visible instead. |
| *"Three fixes in and it's still failing — the next one will land."* | Stop at three failed fixes and question the design. Three wrong fixes is a measurement of your model of the system, and the fourth is drawn from the same wrong model. |
| *"Adding logging would take longer than just trying the fix."* | Add the logging. "Just trying it" burns a build cycle and leaves no residue; instrumentation is what makes the next fix cheaper and the cause visible. |

## Worked example

❌ **What this looks like when it fails:**

> Re-run `report::tests::totals_by_day` alone first to confirm the specific fix,
> then, if time allows before 16:00, run the broader `report` test module too.

✅ **What it looks like when it holds:**

> Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing. Trigger:
> `cargo test report::tests::totals_by_day`, red every run — `left: 13`,
> `right: 14`. I have a guess, `totals.rs:88` filtering `start < ts && ts < end`,
> but I read the fixture before acting on it: walking its timestamps against that
> filter by hand gives 13, and the row it drops is the one stamped exactly at
> `end`. That is the mechanism, and it predicts the assertion exactly — an
> exclusive upper bound on a day-boundary fixture. Minimal fix: make the upper
> bound inclusive at line 88. Re-running the one test — green — then the full
> suite before I report anything. The 16:00 deadline does not decide which tests
> can catch what this fix disturbed.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED once the reproduction can be written as a test. Write
  it, watch it fail, then fix: that red run is both your trigger and your proof.
- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you call the bug
  fixed. The reproduction going green is necessary, not sufficient.
- `drovr:code-review` — REQUIRED once the fix is green, before you call the
  change done.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary. Record the trigger and the
  mechanism there; they are the parts of this that do not survive in the diff.

content.text:
Mechanism confirmed by inode, not inference:

- elephant's watch set includes `/usr/share/applications` (ino `6517`), `~/.local/share/applications` (`43e`), and **profile-2's** `share/applications` (`153634`) — the generation current when it started at 04:04.
- Generations 3, 4 and 5 (`1a9027`, `1c7903`, `1cb882`) are **not** watched.

inotify watches inodes, not paths. A home-manager switch never mutates the watched directory — store paths are immutable — it repoints `~/.nix-profile` at a brand-new directory. So no event ever fires, the new dir is never added, and the index is frozen at profile-2: firefox still listed because it existed then, zen absent because it arrived in profile-5. Restarting the backend should flip both, which is also the proof:

input.command: systemctl --user restart elephant.service && sleep 3; echo "=== zen after restart:"; timeout 30 elephant query "desktopapplications;zen;3" 2>&1 | head -4; echo; echo "=== firefox after restart (should be gone):"; timeout 30 elephant query "desktopapplications;firefox;3" 2>&1 | head -4

content.text:
Fixed, and it wasn't walker — it was `elephant`, walker's data backend.

**Cause:** elephant indexes desktop entries at startup and watches the XDG dirs with inotify, which binds to the *inode* it resolved then. A home-manager switch never mutates that directory — store paths are immutable — it repoints `~/.nix-profile` at a brand-new one. So no event ever fires and the index freezes at whichever generation was current when elephant started. Proof, before any change: elephant (up since 04:04) watched **profile-2's** `share/applications` (ino `153634`) and not profile-3/4/5 (`1a9027`/`1c7903`/`1cb882`), so it still served `firefox.desktop` — gone from disk at 20:36 — and had never seen `zen-beta.desktop`.

**What I did:** `systemctl --user restart elephant.service`. Now `elephant query "desktopapplications;zen;3"` returns `zen-beta.desktop` → "Zen Browser (Beta)", and firefox returns nothing (the client panics with `unexpected end of JSON input` on zero results — same panic for a nonsense query, so that's an elephant client bug, not your config).

Try it: hit walker and type `zen`.

This will recur on every switch, which is worth one declarative line — adding `home.path` to the unit's restart trigger, so home-manager restarts elephant whenever the package set changes:

```nix
systemd.user.services.elephant.Unit.X-Restart-Triggers = [ "${config.home.path}" ];
```

Its unit already carries an `X-Restart-Triggers` hash from the walker module, but that only tracks walker's *config*, which is why three switches went by without a restart.

content.text:
**Why it's there:** nothing asked for it — it's a transitive dependency, twice over.

1. `pacman -Qi avahi` → *"Installed as a dependency"*, `Required By: passim pipewire-pulse`.
2. `passim` is itself a dependency, required by **fwupd** (firmware updates). Passim is fwupd's local caching daemon — it advertises cached metadata to other machines on the LAN over mDNS, which is why it wants avahi.
3. `pipewire-pulse` you installed explicitly; it links avahi for PulseAudio's old "publish/discover audio devices over the network" feature (`module-zeroconf-publish`/`-discover`).

**What avahi does:** it's the Linux Bonjour — an mDNS/DNS-SD daemon. It answers `*.local` names without a DNS server and broadcasts/browses service records on the LAN, which is how printers, Chromecasts, network shares and AirPlay-ish things get discovered automatically. The three desktop entries are its GTK front-ends for browsing those records by hand.

**What it's doing on this box: nothing.**

- `avahi-daemon.service` and `avahi-daemon.socket` are both **disabled**, service **inactive**, and `pgrep` finds zero avahi processes.
- `/etc/nsswitch.conf` has `hosts: mymachines resolve [!UNAVAIL=return] files myhostname dns` — no `mdns_minimal`, so `.local` resolution doesn't go through avahi either (systemd-resolved's own mDNS would be the path, if enabled).

So it's an inert library dependency whose only visible effect is three iconless launcher entries. You can't `pacman -R` it without removing fwupd and pipewire-pulse, so hiding the entries is the right fix rather than uninstalling.

`~/.config/elephant/desktopapplications.toml` supports `blacklist` (list of regexps) — *"blacklist desktop files from being parsed"*. new = '''  programs.walker = lib.optionalAttrs (!isDarwin && isDesktop) {
    enable = true;
    runAsService = true;
    # Arch's avahi ships three GTK mDNS browsers in /usr/share/applications
    # (avahi-discover, bssh, bvnc: "Avahi Zeroconf/SSH/VNC Server Browser").

    # hicolor/Humanity/Yaru*, and none carries that name). The Zeroconf one also
    # fuzzy-matches "zen" through Ze-roco-n-f and outranked the real browser on
    # history score.
    #
    # Blacklist rather than a NoDisplay entry shadowing theirs in
    # ~/.local/share/applications: this is the launcher declining to index them.
    # Matched against the basename with .desktop stripped, anchored because that
    # is what the provider compares — files.go does
    # regexp.MatchString(strings.TrimSuffix(filepath.Base(path), ".desktop")) —
    # so a pattern spelling out `\\.desktop$` silently never matches.
    elephant.provider.desktopapplications.settings.blacklist = [
      "^avahi-discover$"
      "^bssh$"
      "^bvnc$"
    ];
  };

walker: stop indexing avahi's three mDNS browser entries

Arch's avahi ships avahi-discover, bssh and bvnc desktop entries in
/usr/share/applications, and they are noise on this host in three separate ways.

Nothing here wants avahi: `pacman -Qi` reports it installed as a dependency,
required by passim (itself pulled in by fwupd) and pipewire-pulse.
avahi-daemon.service and .socket are both disabled, no avahi process is running,
and /etc/nsswitch.conf carries no mdns entry, so nothing on the box resolves
.local through it either. It cannot be removed without taking fwupd and
pipewire-pulse with it, so the entries are what to deal with.

They also draw no icon. All three declare Icon=network-wired, and no installed
theme provides that name: the host has default, hicolor and locolor, the profile
adds hicolor, Humanity and Yaru*, and a find for network-wired* across all of
them returns nothing. elephant's icon_placeholder does not cover it either,
since that applies to entries with no Icon= at all.

And "Avahi Zeroconf Browser" fuzzy-matches `zen` -- Ze-roco-n-f, which
elephant's own fuzzyinfo confirms at positions 6, 7, 12 -- and outranked the
real browser 90 to 88 on history score, so typing zen offered the mDNS browser
first.

Blacklist rather than NoDisplay entries shadowing theirs from
~/.local/share/applications: this is the launcher declining to index them, not a
second set of desktop files pretending to be the first. The patterns are
anchored basenames with no .desktop suffix because that is what the provider
compares -- files.go:90-93 matches each regexp against
strings.TrimSuffix(filepath.Base(path), ".desktop") -- so the obvious spelling
`^(avahi-discover|bssh|bvnc)\.desktop$` would have been a silent no-op.

Verified against the running backend by dropping the rendered toml in place and
restarting elephant: `elephant query "desktopapplications;zen;3"` then returns
zen-beta.desktop alone, avahi queries return nothing, ghostty still indexes as a
control, and removing the file brings bssh/bvnc straight back. The rendered unit
changes its X-Restart-Triggers hash, so the switch that installs this restarts
elephant rather than leaving a stale index.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
MSG

Two things fall out of that, one of them a correction to my own comment:

- **The icon story I wrote was wrong.** `gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.interface icon-theme` → `'Adwaita'`, and Adwaita is **not installed**, so GTK falls back to hicolor alone. `network-wired.svg` does exist — in Humanity, which is in *Yaru-dark's* inheritance chain (`Inherits=Yaru,Humanity,hicolor`) — but Yaru-dark isn't the active theme at runtime, even though `home.nix:2471` sets it. So the missing icon isn't avahi's fault and isn't a reason to blacklist.
- **Blacklist gap confirmed:** `addNewEntry` on the inotify path calls `parseFile` and stores the result with no blacklist check, so a `pacman` upgrade that rewrites those files re-indexes them until elephant restarts.

walker: stop indexing avahi's three mDNS browser entries

Arch's avahi ships avahi-discover, bssh and bvnc desktop entries in
/usr/share/applications ("Avahi Zeroconf Browser", "Avahi SSH Server Browser",
"Avahi VNC Server Browser"), and nothing on these hosts wants them.

pacman -Qi reports avahi installed as a dependency, required by passim (which
fwupd pulls in) and pipewire-pulse. avahi-daemon.service and .socket are both
disabled, no avahi process runs, and /etc/nsswitch.conf carries no mdns entry,
so not even .local resolution goes through it. The package cannot be removed
without taking fwupd and pipewire-pulse along, so the entries are what to deal
with. "Avahi Zeroconf Browser" also fuzzy-matches `zen` -- Ze-roco-n-f, which
elephant's fuzzyinfo confirms at positions 6, 7, 12 -- which is how it came up
while the browser migration was being tested.

Blacklist rather than NoDisplay entries shadowing theirs from
~/.local/share/applications. Elephant does honor NoDisplay and walks
XDG_DATA_HOME first, so shadowing would have worked; it just means maintaining a
second set of desktop files whose only job is to contradict the first.

The patterns are anchored basenames with no .desktop suffix because that is what
the provider compares: files.go matches each regexp against
strings.TrimSuffix(filepath.Base(path), ".desktop"). The obvious
`^(avahi-discover|bssh|bvnc)\.desktop$` would have been a silent no-op, and an
unanchored `bssh` would also catch a future libbssh-whatever.desktop.

Verified against the running backend by dropping the rendered toml in place and
restarting elephant: `elephant query "desktopapplications;zen;3"` then returns
zen-beta.desktop alone, avahi queries return nothing, ghostty still indexes as a
control, and removing the file brings bssh/bvnc straight back. Both
elephant.service and walker.service change their X-Restart-Triggers hash, so the
switch restarts each of them rather than leaving a stale index -- walker's module
hashes the elephant config into its own trigger.

Two limits, both recorded in the comment:

- Only the startup walk is filtered. addNewEntry, on the inotify path, calls
  parseFile and stores the entry without consulting the blacklist, so a pacman
  upgrade that rewrites one of these files re-indexes it until elephant is
  restarted.
- It applies to every gui host, not only the one the pacman and systemd facts
  were measured on, and is a no-op where the files are absent. Confirmed by
  eval: shiori, setsuna and utsuho change, the two headless hosts and darwin's
  mari do not.

Review corrected two claims an earlier draft of this commit made. The missing
icons are not part of the case against these entries: Icon=network-wired IS
provided by Humanity, which Yaru-dark inherits, and they render blank only
because the theme actually in force is Adwaita (gsettings reads 'Adwaita' even
though gtk.iconTheme asks for Yaru-dark) and no Adwaita theme is installed, so
lookups fall back to hicolor. That is a separate bug affecting every icon name
hicolor lacks. And the "Zeroconf outranks Zen" inversion was a transient
history-score state -- the live query now puts zen-beta first, 91 to 70 -- so the
fuzzy match, not the ranking, is the durable reason.
